topic: How does Wi-Fi go through walls?
title: Why Wi-Fi Goes Through Walls (But Not Metal) 📶
description: Wi-Fi is light you can't see, with waves about 12 cm long — drywall and wood barely slow it down.
Concrete soaks it up, metal reflects it, and water (including you) absorbs it.
sources: NASA Imagine the Universe – The electromagnetic spectrum (radio, microwaves and light are the same radiation): https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/science/toolbox/emspectrum1.html
NASA Earthdata – Electromagnetic spectrum (visible light ≈ 380–700 nm): https://earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/earth-observation-data-basics/electromagnetic-spectrum

beats.narration: Its waves are about *12 centimeters* long, wiggling 2.4 billion times a second.
The light you see? Less than a thousandth of a millimeter.
Waves that big slip through drywall and wood almost untouched.
Thick concrete and brick soak up more, especially on 5 gigahertz.
But metal acts like a *mirror* and bounces it right back.
It's also why your microwave is a metal box: it keeps its waves inside.
And water absorbs it, so your own body blocks the signal too.
Every wall in the way costs signal, and the losses add up.
